courses.title: 1. Understanding Mind and Body
courses.subtitle: Why performance pressure is a protective reaction – not a defect.

lessons.title: Accelerator and Brake
lessons.summary: The dual control model: why desire depends not only on stimulation, but on what is putting on the brakes.
lessons.content:
When your body doesn't respond the way you'd like at the crucial moment – the erection fades, wetness doesn't come, or everything happens far too fast – the first thought is almost always: Something is wrong with me.

Why it works
Sex research describes arousal with a simple image: a car with an accelerator and a brake. The accelerator responds to everything that attracts – closeness, touch, scent, fantasy. The brake responds to everything that sounds like danger – stress, tiredness, shame, worry. Both work in the brain at the same time and independently of each other. The important part: people who feel too little desire usually don't have too little accelerator, but too much brake.
The body follows. For erection and wetness, the nervous system needs rest mode: the blood vessels in the pelvis widen and blood flows in. Under stress the body switches to alarm, stress hormones narrow the vessels, the pelvic floor tightens, and in men ejaculation can come faster.
The brain barely distinguishes between real danger and the thought “I hope it works tonight”. Both press the same brake.

The exercise
Make a small list with two columns. On the left: What presses your accelerator? For example a certain scent, time without hurry, a way of kissing. On the right: What presses the brake? For example an untidy bedroom, the phone, the worry of taking too long.
Look closely at the right-hand column. This program isn't about pressing the accelerator harder, but about learning to take your foot off the brake.

When to see a doctor
If erection or wetness stays away permanently, even without pressure and when you're alone, a medical examination is worthwhile. In men, erectile problems can be an early sign of cardiovascular disease.
lessons.reflection_question: At what moment do you typically feel your system switch from pleasure to tension – and what happened just before?

lessons.title: The Vicious Circle of Anticipatory Anxiety
lessons.summary: How a single experience leads to being in alarm mode before anything starts – and where to break the circle.
lessons.content:
Almost everyone experiences situations where the body doesn't play along – because of tiredness, alcohol, stress or simply not being in the mood. Normally you write it off as a bad day.

Why it works
It only becomes a problem when a single experience is judged as a catastrophe. The next time, you no longer go into the situation with anticipation, but with a silent test question: “Will it happen again?”
That creates a circle. First: an intimate situation begins. Second: the memory triggers tension before anything has happened. Third: you start watching your own body with suspicion. Fourth: the tension presses the brake from the first lesson. Fifth: what you feared happens – and seems to confirm the fear.
Cognitive behavioural therapy starts at the second step: with automatic thoughts. Sentences like “If it doesn't work tonight, I've failed” feel like facts, but they are judgements. And judgements can be checked.

The exercise
Write down the sentence that first goes through your head when closeness is about to happen. Then ask yourself: Is that really true? What would I say to a good friend who thinks this way? Phrase a more realistic sentence, for example: “My body had a bad day. That says nothing about me or our relationship.”
The reframing journal in the app takes you through exactly this exercise step by step.

When to see a doctor
If the anxiety weighs on you heavily or you avoid closeness permanently, sex therapy can be very helpful. That's not a sign of weakness, but a good shortcut.
lessons.reflection_question: Which sentence shoots through your head first when an intimate situation is about to happen – and what would a kinder, more realistic sentence sound like?

lessons.title: Audio Practice: Releasing the Brake
lessons.summary: A guided breathing exercise with a double inhale to signal to the body: there is no danger.
lessons.content:
Make yourself comfortable for the next three minutes. You can sit or lie down. Close your eyes if you like.

We'll now use a simple breathing technique that calms the body particularly quickly: the double inhale with a long exhale. Experts call it the physiological sigh.

Breathe in deeply through your nose. And when you think your lungs are full, take a small second breath on top. Now let the air out very slowly through your slightly open mouth. As long as you can.

Very good. Twice more. Breathe in deeply through your nose. A little sip of air on top. And breathe out long, soft and completely. Feel your shoulders sink a little.

One last time. Breathe in deeply. Top up briefly. And let everything go. Let your lower jaw relax. Release your tongue from the roof of your mouth.

Now simply let your breath flow. Bring your attention to your lower belly. As you breathe in, the abdominal wall gently rises; as you breathe out, everything softly sinks back.

Right now there is nothing to achieve, nothing to check and nothing to reach. Your body may simply become heavy. Stay here for a few more breaths.
lessons.reflection_question: How do your shoulders and jaw feel now compared with three minutes ago?

courses.title: 2. The Anatomy of Arousal
courses.subtitle: More than three zones: how the whole body feels pleasure – and how to find your own map.

lessons.title: Arousal Is a Whole-Body Event
lessons.summary: What happens in the body as pleasure grows – far beyond the genitals.
lessons.content:
When people talk about arousal, most think of three places: penis, breasts and clitoris. Yet arousal is an event of the whole body. It begins in the head, shows on the skin and runs through breath, heart and pelvis.

What happens
The nervous system switches into rest-and-pleasure mode. Blood flows into the erectile tissue, and every body has it: in the penis just as in the clitoris, the labia and around the vaginal opening. Lips, nipples and earlobes also receive more blood and become more sensitive. Breathing deepens, the heart beats faster, and in many people the skin on the chest and neck flushes.
With arousal, the way touch arrives changes too. What felt neutral a moment ago now feels intense.

Why it works
In surveys where people rated their body zone by zone, mouth and lips, breasts and nipples, nape, neck and inner thighs came far ahead after the genitals. Women and men differed much less than many think. And almost every part of the body was named as arousing by someone.
The order matters as well. What is too much at the start can be wonderful in the middle of arousal. That is why it pays to begin with the zones further out and to approach the centre slowly.

The exercise
Take ten minutes and observe your body as pleasure arrives, alone or together. Where does it get warm? Where does it tingle? Where does the skin become more sensitive? Remember three places outside the genitals that respond too.

Consent and safety
Every body responds differently, and the same body responds differently on different days. There is no zone that has to be arousing.
lessons.reflection_question: Which place outside your genitals responds when pleasure arrives – and did you already know?

lessons.title: Head, Ears, Neck and Nape
lessons.summary: Why slow, light touch on the head and neck sets off so much.
lessons.content:
The head is full of nerves. The lips are among the most sensitive places of the body, the scalp feels every hair that moves, and the neck and nape have thin skin that hardly anyone touches in everyday life.

Why it works
In hairy skin, which means almost everywhere except the palms and soles, there are special nerve fibres, the C-tactile fibres. They report less where you are touched and more how it feels. They respond most strongly to slow, light stroking with a hand at skin temperature, a few centimetres per second, which is slower than most people stroke on their own. In studies, people describe such touch as especially pleasant, and many find it calming.
The ear has one more special feature: part of the outer ear is supplied by a small branch of the vagus nerve, a nerve involved in relaxation, among other things. Whether that explains why gentle stroking of the ear feels so cosy to many is not settled. What is certain: the ear is sensitive, and a breath there gives many people goosebumps.

The exercise
Stroke yourself or {P:your partner} from the ear over the neck to the shoulder. First at your usual pace, then half as fast, then half as fast again. Which pace feels the most beautiful?
Also try: fingertips circling over the scalp. A gentle pull on a handful of hair, close to the roots. Lips brushing over the nape without kissing.

Consent and safety
The neck is vulnerable. Pressure on the front of the neck does not belong in an exploration, not even playfully. Some people don't like sounds or wet kisses at the ear. Ask each other.
lessons.reflection_question: Which pace felt the most beautiful – and is it slower than the one you usually touch with?

lessons.title: Back, Belly, Backs of the Knees and Feet
lessons.summary: The forgotten surfaces – and why they in particular can awaken pleasure.
lessons.content:
Back, belly, the backs of the knees and the feet are often skipped during sex. Yet they are large, calm surfaces on which arousal can build well.

Why it works
The back is the largest continuous area of skin, and we can hardly reach it ourselves. Touch there often feels like being held, and for many, feeling held is the door to pleasure. The skin over the sacrum, the flat area above the buttocks, is supplied by nerves from the lower spinal cord, the same region as the pelvic floor and genitals. Some feel warmth and pressure there all the way into the pelvis. Whether that is because of this proximity is not proven – just try how it feels for you.
The lower belly lies over the bladder and the uterus or prostate, close to the inner parts of pleasure. The backs of the knees and the insides of the wrists have thin, soft skin. And the feet are full of nerve endings. Whoever lets them be touched often lets go inside as well.
A frequently heard explanation is that in the brain the feet lie right next to the genitals, which is why they are arousing. Newer measurements suggest, however, that the genitals are represented closer to the hip. So why many people find feet erotic remains open. It is enough that it feels good.

The exercise
Let yourself be touched for ten minutes only on the back, belly, backs of the knees and feet, or touch yourself there. At the end, lay one warm hand flat on the sacrum and the other on the lower belly and breathe between both hands. Notice whether something stirs in the pelvis.

Consent and safety
Feet and the backs of the knees are ticklish for many. Firm, calm pressure then usually helps more than delicate touch. During pregnancy, touch the belly only gently, and if unsure, ask your midwife or doctor.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of these forgotten surfaces would you like to be touched on more often?

lessons.title: Chest, Perineum and Buttocks – in Every Body
lessons.summary: Zones that every body has and that are often attributed to only one sex.
lessons.content:
Nipples are often seen as female, the perineum as an insider tip for men, the buttocks as taboo. In fact every body has these zones, and in every body they can give pleasure.

Why it works
Chest and nipples: in many people, regardless of sex, the nipples become erect when touched, and some feel it all the way into the pelvis. A small brain-imaging study in women found that touching the nipple also stimulated the brain area where touch to the genitals arrives. That is an interesting clue, but no proof that it is the same for everyone. Many men also enjoy being touched on the chest but don't dare to say so.
The perineum, the place between the genitals and the anus: the pudendal nerve, which also supplies the genitals, runs here. In people with a penis the root of the penis lies beneath it; in people with a vulva, erectile tissue and the legs of the clitoris lie there. Gentle pressure from outside reaches these deep parts.
The buttocks and the anus: the skin around the anus is densely packed with nerve endings. For some, a flat, warm hand on the buttocks is already enough; others like more. Both are fine, and none of it has to happen.

The exercise
Explore the chest with different kinds of touch: a flat hand, fingertips circling around the areola, a light tug, a breath of air. Then the perineum: lay two fingers flat, press gently, release, small circles. Notice how your pelvic floor responds.

Consent and safety
Nipples are very sensitive for some people, for example before a period or while breastfeeding. At the anus, always use lubricant and short nails, and never move from the anus to the vulva or into the vagina without first washing hands or toys. More on this in course 11.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of these zones have you so far not credited your own body with?

lessons.title: Your Own Map
lessons.summary: Draw a body map of your pleasure – and swap it with your partner if you like.
lessons.content:
Textbooks show an average map. Only you know your own map, and often not even you. Drawing it is one of the most beautiful ways to get to know yourself.

Why it works
Whoever knows which zones carry them can rely on them in an encounter and doesn't have to guess. And whoever knows their partner's map touches with more confidence and less pressure.
The map changes: with the cycle, mood, age and level of arousal. A place that is unpleasant at the start can later be the most beautiful.

The exercise
Draw two simple outlines on a sheet of paper, from the front and from the back. Then explore your body zone by zone, for example with the guided self-exploration. Afterwards, colour it in: green for “very much”, yellow for “sometimes” or “only later”, red for “rather not”. Write down what kind of touch you like in a place: light, firm, warm, slow.
If you are in a relationship: ask {P:your partner} to draw a map too. Swap them and tell each other what surprised you. Then try out a green spot on the other's map that you have never touched before.

Consent and safety
Red stays red until the person changes it themselves. A map is an invitation, not a contract, and today may be different from yesterday.
lessons.reflection_question: Which place on your map surprised you?

courses.title: 3. Every Body Is Beautiful and Sexy
courses.subtitle: Out of comparison, into feeling: how women and men can see their bodies with kind eyes and feel desirable in them.

lessons.title: The Myth of the Perfect Body
lessons.summary: Where the idea of the “right” body comes from, and how varied the bodies of women and men really are.
lessons.content:
Most of the bodies we see every day have been carefully selected, well lit and often edited. In advertising, on social media, in films and in porn, they show only a tiny slice of what people actually look like. Anyone who measures themselves against that can only lose. That's as true for women as it is for men, even though the ideals differ.

Two ideals, one problem
Women are often shown a slim, firm, smooth body: a flat belly, firm breasts, not a trace of cellulite, no hair except on the head. Men are often shown a tall, muscular body: broad shoulders, a six-pack, full hair, a big penis. Both ideals have one thing in common: very few people look like that, and even they often only with good lighting, the right pose and photo editing.

How varied bodies really are
Skin: it has pores, moles, freckles, spots, redness, scars and stretch marks, in women and men alike. The vast majority of women have cellulite, including very slim women.
Hair: everyone grows body hair, sometimes thick, sometimes sparse, on the legs, armpits, belly, chest, back and around the genitals. Many men lose hair on their head over the years; that's very common and not a weakness.
Belly and bottom: bellies are round, soft, and have folds or rolls when you sit. Bottoms are flat or round, firm or soft.
Chest: breasts differ in size and shape, often even the two breasts of the same woman. Nipples are light or dark, large or small, flat or protruding. Men have a chest too, which can be flat, muscular or soft.
Height and build: bodies are tall or short, narrow or broad, sturdy or slight. None of these shapes is naturally more attractive than another.
Genitals: labia can be short or long, and the two sides are usually different. Penises are straight or curved. When soft they are sometimes smaller, sometimes larger, and that says little about how big they get when aroused. Testicles often hang at different heights.
All of this is normal, not the exception.

Why comparison hurts so much
Our brain compares automatically. Seeing lots of edited images quietly shifts our inner yardstick. At some point your own, perfectly normal body starts to look like a mistake. So the problem isn't your body, it's the yardstick you measure it against.
On top of that: anyone who struggles with how they look is often half in their head during sex. Instead of feeling, they watch themselves. That costs pleasure, which is exactly why it's worth changing this way of looking.

The task
For one week, notice which body images you come across: on your phone, in ads, in films. Each time, briefly ask yourself: is this real or staged? And what feeling does this image stir in me?
If you like, also follow a few people or projects that show real, unedited bodies, of women and of men. Many find that this changes how they see themselves, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which image of a “right” body do you carry around with you, and where does it come from?

lessons.title: A Kind Look in the Mirror
lessons.summary: Describing instead of judging: a mirror exercise for women and men that quietens the inner critic.
lessons.content:
Many people look in the mirror like a strict inspector: what's wrong, what's too much, what's too little? For women this gaze often lands on the belly, thighs, bottom and skin. For men on the belly, muscles, height, hairline and penis. This critical gaze is learned, and it can be unlearned too.

Describing instead of judging
The first step isn't to find everything beautiful. That would be asking too much. The first step is to look neutrally. Experts call this body neutrality: seeing your body as it is, without judgement.
Instead of “my belly is too fat”, you say: “My belly is round and soft.”
Instead of “my thighs are awful”: “My thighs are strong and carry me.”
Instead of “I hardly have any muscles”: “My arms are slim.”
Instead of “my hair is getting thin”: “My hair is shorter and lighter than it used to be.”
Neutrality is a bridge between rejection and affection. Once you stop putting yourself down, there's room for kindness.

The task
Stand in front of a mirror for ten minutes, clothed or naked, whatever feels right for you. Make sure the light is pleasant and nobody will disturb you.
Let your gaze wander slowly from top to bottom: hair, face, neck, shoulders, chest, arms, hands, belly, hips, bottom, genitals, thighs, knees, calves, feet. Describe each part in one neutral sentence, out loud or silently.
When a judgement comes up, notice it without condemning yourself for it, and rephrase it neutrally.
Finally, name three things you like about your body and three things you're grateful to it for. For example: my hands can be tender. My legs carried me to work today. My skin feels every touch.

If it's hard
That's normal, especially at first. Start with five minutes. Repeat the exercise a few days in a row. Many notice after a week that the inner critic gets quieter and they pick at themselves less in everyday life.
If looking in the mirror weighs on you heavily, for example if you spend hours preoccupied with one body part or withdraw because of it, talk to a doctor or a psychotherapist. There's good help for this.

Going deeper
The guided body journey below this lesson continues the exercise with your hands: feeling instead of looking.
lessons.reflection_question: Which neutral sentence about your body felt surprisingly good?

lessons.title: Sexy Is a Feeling, Not a Measurement
lessons.summary: What attraction really is about, and how women and men can feel desirable in their bodies.
lessons.content:
Who we find attractive depends surprisingly little on measurements. Presence, a look, a laugh, a voice, the way someone moves and how someone smells: those are the things people remember. And the most important part: feeling sexy is something you can learn, regardless of dress size, height or muscles.

What attraction is about
Many people say they fell in love with someone who wasn't their “type” at all. Attraction arises in contact: when someone feels seen, when someone is relaxed and genuine, when there's humour and warmth. Self-assurance often has a stronger effect than any detail of the body. And self-assurance doesn't mean finding yourself perfect, it means not constantly hiding.

What makes you feel sexy
For some it's a particular piece of clothing: lace, a well-fitting shirt, jeans you feel good in. For others music, dancing, a scent, freshly washed hair, a well-groomed beard or simply a well-rested morning. For some it's movement: sport, yoga, a walk after which you can feel your own muscles.
It isn't about how you look to others, but about how you feel in your body.

The task
Write a list of five things that make you feel sexy or alive. Choose two and do them deliberately this week, just for you. A few ideas:
Wear underwear that feels good, even if nobody sees it.
Dance in the kitchen to a song that moves you.
Take time for body care: lotion, shaving or deliberately not shaving, a warm bath.
Walk more upright for a day, with a soft belly, relaxed shoulders and an open chest.
Look at a photo of yourself where you liked how you looked, and ask yourself what you felt back then.

The body thinks along
Posture and feeling are linked. Standing tall, letting your shoulders drop and breathing deep into your belly often changes how you feel inside too. Sucking in your belly and holding your breath, on the other hand, keeps you tense. Try both deliberately and notice what they do to you.

For couples
For one week, give each other a compliment about the other's body every day, and make it concrete: not “you look good”, but “I love how your shoulders look when you stretch”. Whoever receives the compliment just says “thank you”, without playing it down.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of the five things on your list makes you feel most like yourself?

lessons.title: Lights On: Letting Go of Shame in Bed
lessons.summary: When the light has to go off or the blanket has to stay on: how women and men can quieten shame together.
lessons.content:
Many people can only half enjoy sex because part of their attention is somewhere else. Women suck in their belly, hold on to the blanket or avoid positions in which they find their body “unflattering”. Men worry whether their penis is big enough, whether the erection will last, whether their belly is in the way, or whether they look too hairy or not muscular enough in the light. This self-watching costs arousal. The less you watch yourself, the more you can feel.

What really counts
Often your partner pays attention to completely different things than you do: to closeness, to desire and to you letting go. The belly you see so critically is often simply part of the person they desire. Many people say their partner's insecurity bothers them more than any supposed problem zone, because they want the other to feel good.

Talking about it
Shame gets quieter when you say it out loud. In a calm moment, not in bed, tell each other which parts of your body make you feel insecure. Then the other says what they like about exactly these parts, or simply find normal. Listening is enough, without contradicting or sugar-coating.

The task for two
Take an evening with warm, dimmed light. Undress each other slowly. Whoever is undressing says one sentence with each piece of clothing about what they find beautiful or attractive about the part that's just been revealed. Whoever is being undressed says nothing except “thank you”. Then you swap.
When you're both naked, lie down next to each other and stroke each other for a few minutes with just your eyes and fingertips, without a goal.

If it's too much
Start smaller: candlelight instead of the ceiling lamp, a shirt that may stay on, or one part per evening. There's no obligation to have the light on. There's only the invitation to show a little more of yourselves, bit by bit.

For singles
The exercise also works alone in front of the mirror: undress slowly and give each part that's revealed a kind sentence. And for the next time with someone new, this thought may help: nobody expects a perfect body, only a person who is truly present.
lessons.reflection_question: What surprised you most about what your partner finds beautiful about you?

lessons.title: When Your Body Changes
lessons.summary: Pregnancy, ageing, illness, scars: how women and men can stay kind to their bodies, even as they change.
lessons.content:
No body stays the same. Life leaves its marks, on women and on men. Sometimes your own body feels foreign afterwards, and that can affect desire too.

What can change
For women: after pregnancy, the belly, breasts and skin often change, and stretch marks or a caesarean scar remain. During menopause, skin, weight, hair and vaginal moisture change.
For men: over the years, hair on the head often thins, the belly gets rounder, the muscles get softer. Erections take more time or more direct touch. After prostate surgery or with some medications, erection and ejaculation can change.
For everyone: weight changes, operations, accidents, chronic illnesses, breast surgery, a stoma, scars and skin changes. And simply ageing, with wrinkles, age spots and grey hair.

Grief is allowed
If you miss a body you used to have, that's allowed. Forbidding yourself this grief or brushing it off with “just be grateful” doesn't help. Acknowledging it often clears the way to making friends with the body you have today.

Your body has been through something
A scar tells of an operation that helped. A belly of a child it carried. Wrinkles of many years of laughing. Grey hair of a life that has been lived. You don't have to find that beautiful. But you can acknowledge what your body has carried and come through.

Desire changes, it doesn't disappear
Many couples discover new forms of closeness precisely after changes: more time, more touch across the whole body, less fixation on the same old routine. Those who stay curious often find paths they never had in view before.

The task
Place a hand on a part that has changed or that you struggle with. Breathe calmly into it a few times. Say silently: “Thank you for carrying me through all of this.” If it feels right, stroke it slowly with a little oil. If you're in a relationship, you can invite your partner to touch this part together with you.

Good to know
Changes can affect sexuality too, for example altered sensation after an operation, dryness during menopause or erection problems. Much of this can be treated well, for example with lubricants, local hormones, medication or pelvic floor training. Talk to a doctor if something is weighing on you. It isn't an embarrassing topic, it's everyday business in any practice.
lessons.reflection_question: What can you thank your body for today, even if you don't like everything about it?

lessons.title: Wrapped up: lingerie for every body
lessons.summary: Sexy lingerie isn't just for models: how women and men find underwear they like themselves in.
lessons.content:
Sexy lingerie has a reputation, as if it were made only for young, slim women who look like the ads. Yet it is there for every body: for women and men, for every size and every age. Good lingerie doesn't hide a body, it frames it. And most importantly: it should feel good to you first.

Why lingerie can change so much
What we wear on our skin changes how we move and how we feel. Many people say that in beautiful underwear they walk differently, sit up straighter and look at themselves more kindly in the mirror. That holds true even when nobody else sees it.

For women
There is much more than the classic push-up bra. Soft bralettes without underwire, bodysuits that flatter the whole upper body, camisoles of silk or satin, high-cut briefs that make the legs look longer, lace, mesh, stockings with suspenders. Good shops and brands offer lingerie in many sizes, including for large breasts, wide hips and round bellies. Many women with a soft belly feel especially good in high-waisted briefs or a bodysuit. Others love to show their belly.

For men
Men have more options than grey boxer shorts, too. Snug trunks, skimpy briefs, underwear made of mesh or sheer fabric, silk shorts, an open shirt over bare skin. For many men the thought of dressing up for their partner is unfamiliar. Yet many partners find exactly that very attractive: that he makes an effort and wants to show himself.

How to find what suits you
The size: underwear that pinches or cuts in doesn't feel sexy. Get advice or measure yourself. Sizes vary a lot from brand to brand.
The fabric: silk and satin are cool and smooth, lace is playful, cotton is soft, mesh is cheeky. Touch the fabric and imagine how it will feel for a whole evening.
The colour: black and red are classics. Dark green, burgundy, midnight blue or a shade close to your skin tone can be just as beautiful.
Your favourite spot: which part of yourself do you like? Your bottom, your back, your shoulders, your chest, your legs? Look for lingerie that shows off exactly that spot.

The exercise
Pick a piece of lingerie you would never normally buy and try it on, in the shop or at home in front of the mirror. Don't pay attention to what bothers you, but to what it does to your posture. Then wear it for a whole day under your normal clothes. Nobody needs to know.

For couples
Choose lingerie together, in a shop or on the sofa. Each person picks one piece for themselves and one for the other. Anyone who doesn't want to wear something says so, and it isn't up for discussion. And don't forget the men: he gets to be wrapped up nicely, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which piece of lingerie surprised you by how good you felt in it, and which part of you did it show off?

courses.title: 4. Escaping the Spectator Trap
courses.subtitle: How to stop checking yourself from the outside during sex – and get back to feeling.

lessons.title: The Spectator Trap
lessons.summary: Why self-observation during sex works like a director switching on the floodlights in the middle of the scene.
lessons.content:
As early as the 1970s, the sex researchers Masters and Johnson described a pattern that is still one of the most important keys to performance pressure – in men as in women. They called it spectatoring. A good everyday name for it: the spectator trap.

Why it works
When you are aroused, you are normally right in the middle of it: you feel warmth, skin, scent, movement. The brooding, planning part of the brain gets quieter.
In the spectator trap the opposite happens. Inwardly you step next to the bed and watch yourself with a clipboard: “Is my body working right now? Am I taking too long, is it too fast? How do I look? What is my partner thinking?”
The tricky part: checking whether you're aroused disturbs exactly what arousal needs – letting go in the moment. Arousal can no more be forced than falling asleep. The more you control, the cooler the feeling gets. And the observing itself presses the brake from course 1.

The exercise
Get to know your inner examiner. After your next intimate encounter, or after time on your own, note down: What questions did it ask? What did it pay attention to?
Give it a name, preferably a slightly ridiculous one. Once you recognise your examiner, you can greet it kindly next time – and turn back to what there is to feel right now. The next lesson shows how.
lessons.reflection_question: What does your inner examiner focus on most when you slip into the spectator trap?

lessons.title: Feeling Instead of Checking: The Art of Attention
lessons.summary: How to steer your attention away from brooding and back into your senses – with three simple anchors.
lessons.content:
How do you get out of your head and back into your body when the inner examiner is already talking loudly? The advice “just don't think about it” doesn't help – anyone who tries not to think of a pink elephant sees one immediately.

Why it works
Attention has limited space. If you direct it fully onto one concrete sensation, less is left over for worrying thoughts. This is the core of sensate focus, the touch exercises developed by Masters and Johnson, and one of the best-researched methods in sex therapy.
What matters: the point is not to create arousal through touch. Touching to test whether it arouses you is already the spectator trap again. You feel just to feel. Arousal often comes by itself precisely when it is no longer the goal.

The exercise
As soon as you notice you're drifting off in your head, pick three qualities of the touch that is happening right now:
First, temperature: Where is the skin warm, where is it cool?
Second, texture: smooth, soft, rough, moist?
Third, pressure: How firm is the contact right now?

courses.title: 5. Pain, Shame and Performance Pressure

lessons.title: When Sex Hurts
lessons.summary: Pain during sex is common, has causes and can be treated. Enduring it is not the way.
lessons.content:
Many people know pain during sex, especially often women and other people with a vulva, some only occasionally, some every time. Often they stay silent about it for a long time, out of shame or out of worry about disappointing their partner. Yet pain is a signal, not a part of sex you have to endure.

Why this happens
The causes are varied: too little lubrication or arousal, infections, skin changes, scars, endometriosis, hormonal changes after giving birth or in menopause. A tense pelvic floor is also very common.
On top of that there's a circle: expecting pain makes you tense up. A tense pelvic floor makes penetration more painful. The next pain confirms the expectation. For some, the muscles at the vaginal entrance cramp so strongly that penetration isn't possible at all. This is called vaginismus, and it too can be treated well.

The exercise
First: agree on a break from penetration. Everything else stays allowed. That takes the fear out of every touch.
Second: learn to release the pelvic floor. The letting-go exercise in the pelvic floor timer is made for this: breathe in, widen, yield.
Third: when penetration is added again, the person who had the pain decides everything: whether, when, how deep, how fast. Plenty of lubricant, positions in which she is on top, and stop at any time. Pain doesn't have to be endured, not even for your partner's sake. A pause, stopping, or a different kind of closeness are always okay.

Consent and safety
Have pain checked by a doctor, for example a gynaecologist, especially if it's new, strong, burns, bleeds, keeps coming back or persists. Pelvic floor physiotherapy and sex therapy are very effective for pain and vaginismus. Please use aids such as dilators only with professional guidance.

lessons.title: When the Erection Doesn't Play Along
lessons.summary: A missing erection is usually not a defect, but stress at the wrong moment.
lessons.content:
Most men experience at some point that the erection doesn't come or disappears. Once is often enough for the worry to come along next time. And precisely this worry makes it more likely to happen again.

Why this happens
An erection needs relaxation. The nervous system has to be in rest mode so blood can flow in. Anxiety, pressure and self-observation switch to alarm mode. That's the spectator trap from course 4: whoever checks whether they're hard enough is no longer with the pleasure.
A possible clue: if erections in the morning or when alone are as usual, that suggests tension or the situation play a big part. It doesn't rule out physical causes, though, and often both work together. If they're missing permanently, the body should be examined by a doctor.

The exercise
First: agree on sex without an erection. For a few encounters, penetration is explicitly not on the agenda. Hands, mouth, skin, time. When nothing has to stand up, it often does by itself – and if not, nothing is lost.
Second: check your thoughts. Write sentences like “If I fail, she'll leave me” in the thought journal and ask yourself whether they're true.
Third: talk about it. Many partners relate a missing erection to themselves. A sentence like “It has nothing to do with you, my head was loud” relieves you both.

Consent and safety
Erectile problems can be an early sign of heart and vascular disease. Have them checked by a doctor if they persist, keep coming back or weigh on you. Erectile dysfunction medication only after medical advice and never together with nitrates.

lessons.title: Coming Too Soon: Control Through Relaxation

Why this happens
Orgasm comes when arousal crosses a threshold. Tension, shallow breathing and a tight pelvic floor make arousal rise faster. Breathing calmly and keeping the pelvic floor loose, on the other hand, gives you more room.
On top of that there's habit. Anyone who has reached the goal quickly for years, for example when masturbating, has learned it as a pattern. Patterns can be relearned.

The exercise
First: practise alone with the stop-start method. Touch yourself until arousal is high, but not yet just before the point of no return. Then stop, breathe out, release the pelvic floor, wait until arousal drops a little. Repeat three or four times, then you may come.
Second: perceive arousal as a scale from one to ten. The aim is to stay in the six to seven range for a long time.
Third: practise together, first with hands, then during sex with slow, deep movements instead of fast ones. Pauses are allowed and can be very sensual.

Consent and safety
If you've always come very quickly or it distresses you a lot, talk to a urologist or a sex therapist. Effective treatments exist. And: sex doesn't end with your orgasm. Hands and mouth remain.

lessons.title: Shame: When Your Own Body Gets in the Way

Pulling in your belly, lights off, avoiding certain positions, keeping wishes to yourself: shame often lies in bed with you during sex. It costs desire, because part of your attention is busy with how you look or what the other might think.

Why this happens
Shame is a social feeling. It arises from comparisons and judgements we've often carried for a long time: from family, from the media, from earlier experiences. In bed it becomes the brake from course 1 and the spectator trap from course 4 at the same time.
The good news: during sex, partners usually see each other's bodies far more kindly than we see ourselves. Desire looks at aliveness, not at flaws.

The exercise
First: listen to the inner critic. Write down the sentences that come up in your head during sex, for example “My belly is too fat” or “That's perverted”. The thought journal helps you check them.
Second: reclaim one spot. Choose a part of your body you don't like showing. At the next touch, let it be touched on purpose and keep breathing calmly.
Third: voice one wish, even a small one. The yes/no/maybe list in the couple channel makes this easier, because only what you both want becomes visible.

Consent and safety
Shame can also be connected to distressing experiences. If memories come up that overwhelm you, it's wise to look at them with a psychotherapist. You set the pace.

Many people only undress in the dark, keep their belly pulled in or hope that certain spots won't be touched. Women often struggle with their belly, breasts or skin; men with the size of their penis, their hair, or the fact that at forty-five the erection no longer comes by itself the way it did at eighteen.

Why it works
Shame about your own body is one of the most reliable brakes from course 1. Anyone who watches and judges themselves is in the spectator trap from course 4 – and feels less.
Yet a simple question is worth asking: When did you last lose desire because your partner had a small fold on their belly? Probably never. What attracts us to another person is rarely perfection, but tangible desire: how someone closes their eyes when you kiss their neck. How a hand pulls us closer. The exercise

You don't have to show anything you're not ready for yet. Self-compassion also means respecting your pace. If thoughts about your body weigh on you heavily or dominate your everyday life, psychotherapeutic support can be a great relief.

lessons.title: Erotic Maturity: What Gets Better With the Years

Why it works

courses.title: 7. Pelvic Floor: Letting Go and Strength

lessons.title: Too Tight Rather Than Too Weak

lessons.content:
Anyone looking for pelvic floor exercises almost always comes across the same advice: tighten as often and as hard as possible. That helps many people – for example after giving birth or with bladder weakness. For others it makes the problem worse.

Why it works
With stress, long periods of sitting and performance pressure, the pelvic floor is often not too weak but too tense. Specialists speak of a hypertonic pelvic floor. It is constantly switched on.
Imagine holding your upper arm half-tensed all day. After a few hours the muscle is tired, poorly supplied with blood and can no longer build up targeted strength at the crucial moment.
In the pelvis this can look like this: in women, pain on penetration, a feeling of tightness or an involuntary contraction. In men, fast ejaculation or an erection that comes and goes. In both, often a dull feeling of pressure and less sensation.
A healthy pelvic floor is not as strong as possible, but mobile: it can contract powerfully – and above all let go completely.

The exercise
Feel into your pelvic floor right now, the area between pubic bone and tailbone. Is it soft? Or are you holding a slight base tension there?

With pain in the pelvis or during sex, with incontinence, or if you're unsure whether your pelvic floor is too weak or too tight, specialised pelvic floor physiotherapy helps. It can examine this precisely.

lessons.title: Contracting and Opening: Two Movements

lessons.content:
For the training in the app's pelvic floor timer to work, you need two opposite movements that you learn to tell apart clearly.

Why it works
As you breathe in, the diaphragm descends and the pelvic floor moves down with it. As you breathe out, both rise again. Once you feel this connection, you can steer the pelvic floor through your breath – strengthening it when it needs support and letting go when tension is in the way.

The exercise

Don't regularly train your pelvic floor while actually urinating; that can disturb bladder emptying. If you feel pain when contracting, leave out the strengthening and focus on opening.

The pelvic floor doesn't work on its own. Through muscles and connective tissue it is closely linked to the inner thighs, the hip muscles and the deep hip flexor.

Why it works

lessons.summary: Why many women have a pelvic floor that tends to be too tense – and how targeted opening can help.
lessons.content:
In fitness and postnatal classes, women almost always hear: contract, strengthen! After giving birth or with bladder weakness that is often exactly right. In sex therapy, though, the opposite picture often shows up: a pelvic floor that holds on too much.

Why it works
A permanently tense pelvic floor can have consequences. First: pain on penetration or an involuntary contraction of the muscles at the vaginal entrance, known as vaginismus. Second: less sensation, because a tense muscle is less well supplied with blood. Third: for some women orgasm is also harder to reach, because the muscle has little room for the rhythmic contractions.
On top of that comes the circle from course 1: if you expect pain, you tense up – and if you tense up, you feel more pain.

The exercise
Opening. Breathe deeply into your belly. As you breathe in, imagine the vaginal entrance and perineum becoming soft and gently yielding downwards and outwards, like a bud opening in the warmth. No pushing, just yielding. As you breathe out, everything stays soft.
Practise this for a few minutes every day, also with the pelvic floor timer. Over time, opening becomes something you can call on in intimate moments too.

When to see a doctor
Pain during sex, burning, or penetration not being possible at all can be treated well – but not with an app alone. A gynaecological examination and specialised pelvic floor physiotherapy can achieve a great deal.
lessons.reflection_question: In everyday life or when being touched, can you feel whether your pelvic floor softly yields or unconsciously closes up protectively?

lessons.title: Mental Movies and the Pressure to Be Quick Enough
lessons.summary: How the worry of taking too long or having to orgasm slows desire – and what really awakens it.
lessons.content:
Women often experience performance pressure more quietly, but no less paralysing. While many men fear coming too soon or losing their erection, many women's mental movie circles around similar questions: “I'm taking too long, my partner is getting impatient.” “What do I look like in this position?” “I have to come now so he feels validated.”

Why it works
The sex educator Emily Nagoski has popularised two ideas that take a lot of pressure off here.
First: desire can arise in two ways. Spontaneous desire appears seemingly out of nowhere. Responsive desire only emerges in the encounter, through closeness and touch. Both are normal, in women and in men – but women experience responsive desire much more often. Anyone waiting to feel desire out of nowhere often waits in vain – and wrongly considers themselves lacking in desire.
Second: desire usually grows not through more stimulation, but through fewer brakes, entirely in the spirit of course 1. Stress, tiredness, to-do lists and shame put on the brakes. Safety, time and permission release them.

The exercise
Give yourself explicit permission, out loud or on paper: “I may take all the time my body needs. I don't have to come.”
And look at your most important brake: What would have to be different for you to feel more relaxed in that moment? A thought about it belongs in the reframing journal.
lessons.reflection_question: Which expectation or thought is your biggest inner brake when it comes to your own desire?

lessons.title: The Clitoris: Bigger Than You Think
lessons.summary: Why the clitoris is a whole system of erectile tissue – and why it takes time to awaken.
lessons.content:
The idea still persists that the clitoris is a small point at the top of the labia. In fact, the visible part is only the tip.

Why it works
The clitoris is a system of erectile tissue around ten centimetres long. Its legs and bulbs reach deep into the tissue beneath the labia and surround the vaginal entrance. Like the penis, it consists of tissue that fills with blood.
For that to happen, it needs the same as an erection: a relaxed nervous system and time. For many women it takes considerably longer than a few minutes until the whole system is filled with blood, sensitive and soft. If penetration happens before that, it quickly feels chafing or unpleasant.
So the long time isn't “taking too long”. It's anatomy.

The exercise
Allow yourself, alone or together, to plan this time in explicitly. Don't begin at the tip, but around it: mons, labia, inner thighs. Course 18 shows exactly how, with an illustration.
Pay attention to the changes: warmth, fullness, wetness. They tell you when your body is ready – not the clock.
lessons.reflection_question: How does it feel to think that plenty of time isn't a long wait, but simply anatomy?

lessons.title: The Cycle and Desire
lessons.summary: How hormones can change desire over the month – and why fluctuations are normal.
lessons.content:
Expecting to feel the same desire on every day of the month puts you under unnecessary pressure. For many women, desire changes with the cycle.

Why it works
Roughly, four phases can be described. But experience is very individual, and hormonal contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding or menopause change the picture considerably.
During menstruation some women tend to withdraw, others experience a special sensitivity precisely then.
In the days afterwards oestrogen rises. Many feel more energy and curiosity.
Around ovulation many women experience their strongest desire; the body is often wetter then too.
In the second half of the cycle progesterone dominates. For many, desire shifts from passion towards security and closeness. Pressure and hurry are especially disruptive now.
When couples know about these fluctuations, the feeling “something is wrong with me” often disappears. There are times for fire and times for embers.

The exercise
For two or three months, observe your desire and mood, for example with the app's daily check-in or a cycle app. Is there a pattern? Share it with your partner if you like.

When to see a doctor
Severe pain during your period, sudden persistent lack of desire or menopausal symptoms are a good reason for a conversation with a gynaecologist.
lessons.reflection_question: In which phase of your cycle do you most feel like passion, and when more like security and comfort?

courses.title: 10. Resetting Your Stimulation
courses.subtitle: How fast digital habits can change sensation – and how to retune your ability to feel.

lessons.title: Fast Stimuli and the Reward System
lessons.summary: Why the brain gets used to fast, changing stimuli – and why real closeness needs a different pace.
lessons.content:
For most of human history, sexual stimuli were rare and tied to real encounters. Today an unlimited amount of images and videos is available on the phone at any time.

Why it works
The brain's reward system reacts especially to what is new and unexpected. Clicking from video to video while alone delivers constant new stimuli. The research on this is not clear-cut, and pornography is not automatically a problem. But many men report that real closeness then feels less intense to them.
Two habits can play a role. First: the brain adjusts to fast image changes from a spectator's perspective instead of slow stimuli like scent, skin and closeness. Second: if time alone is mainly used to relieve stress quickly, the body learns: arousal means getting to the goal fast, with a firm grip. That fits the death-grip pattern from course 19.
In a real encounter the familiar pace is then missing, and the nervous system reacts with uncertainty.

The exercise
For one week, observe without judgement: When do you reach for fast digital stimuli? Out of boredom, after stress, out of habit before going to sleep?
Then try, for a few weeks, spending time with yourself without a screen. The next lesson shows how that can work.

When to see a doctor
If you notice that you can no longer control your consumption and it weighs on you, counselling or therapy can help a lot.
lessons.reflection_question: What is your most common reason for reaching for fast digital stimuli in everyday life – and what would you actually need in that moment?

lessons.title: Time With Yourself, Rethought
lessons.summary: From quick stress relief to mindful feeling – four simple rules.
lessons.content:
Time with yourself is not an enemy but your best practice ground – if you change the rules of the game. Instead of a quick sprint to orgasm, it becomes a relaxed journey of discovery.

Why it works
What you practise alone, you take into encounters with a partner. If you enjoy yourself slowly, sensitively and with a soft pelvic floor when alone, you'll find it easier with someone else too. And if you learn to read your own arousal early, you gain stamina without feeling less.

The exercise
Four rules for the coming weeks.
First: no screen. The phone stays outside. Just your body and your imagination.
Second: soft instead of firm. Pay attention to your buttocks and pelvic floor. As soon as you notice you're tensing to push arousal higher, breathe in deeply and consciously let go. And switch from a tight fist to an open, oiled hand.
Third: the scale from one to ten. Stay in the range between six and eight. At seven or eight, slow down and breathe calmly until you're back at about five. Then the next wave.
Fourth: no goal. Take ten to fifteen minutes. Orgasm may come, but it doesn't have to. The pelvic floor timer helps you practise letting go.

Consent and safety
This exercise is just for you. If you're in a relationship, it can be a relief to talk about what you're practising.
lessons.reflection_question: What changes in your sensations when you leave out the screen and deliberately halve the pace?

lessons.title: Audio Practice: Waves Instead of a Sprint
lessons.summary: A guided exercise for time alone: slowly, without a screen, with conscious letting go.
lessons.content:
You do this exercise alone, in a quiet place, with no phone within reach. Have some oil or lubricant ready. I'll guide you. You can stop at any time.

Lie down comfortably. Close your eyes. Breathe deeply into your belly three times and out again slowly. With every exhale your pelvis becomes a little heavier.
Notice how your jaw feels. Let it relax. Let your tongue lie softly in your mouth. Release your buttocks. Release your pelvic floor, as if it were sinking downwards.

Now begin to touch yourself. Not where it has the strongest effect, but around it: belly, inner thighs, groin. Slowly. With an open hand, not a fist.
When you turn to your penis, take your time. Glide long and slow. Feel the warmth of your hand.

Imagine a scale from one to ten. One is completely calm, ten is the point of no return. Where are you right now? You don't need to change anything. Just notice.

Let your arousal rise, slowly, to about seven.
And now: hands still. Breathe out long. Consciously release your pelvic floor. Feel the wave ebb a little, to about five.
That's it.

Begin again. Slowly. Let the wave rise again. Notice whether you tense up to move forward faster. If so: breathe out, let go, carry on at a calm pace.
At seven: hold still again. Breathe out. Let go. Wait.

One more wave. Perhaps you notice that you can now hold seven for longer without it tipping over. That's exactly what you're training: reading and steering your arousal, with relaxation instead of tension.

From now on the time is yours. You may carry on, you may come, you may also simply stop and feel what's there. There is no goal.

When you're done, place a hand on your belly. Breathe calmly. Feel how your body feels now. Thank yourself for this time.
lessons.reflection_question: At which number on the scale do you notice that you start to tense up?

courses.title: 11. Prostate and Perineum: Anatomy and Approach
courses.subtitle: Why the area behind the scrotum can be a source of deep relaxation and pleasure – and how to approach it safely and without shame.

lessons.title: Anatomy Without Shame
lessons.summary: What the prostate is, why touching it feels different from the glans – and why that has nothing to do with sexual orientation.
lessons.content:
Hardly any area of the male body is as loaded with shame as the one behind the scrotum. Many men tense up at the mere thought of being touched there – because of cultural clichés or the worry about what it might say about them. The answer is simple: it says something about anatomy, not about orientation.

Why it works
The prostate is a gland about the size of a chestnut, located directly below the bladder and surrounding the urethra. In developmental terms it is related to the glands on the front wall of the vagina that are often described as the G-area in women.
Through its nerves, the glans delivers fast, sharply defined stimuli. The prostate, by contrast, is embedded in a dense network of nerves in the pelvis. That's why many men describe touch there as deep, warm and filling the whole lower body rather than pinpointed.
There's also a somatic aspect: part of the pelvic floor lies around the prostate. Learning to soften there teaches a lot about the tension that often plays a role in erectile problems and early ejaculation – see course 7 and course 19.
Some men experience orgasms through the prostate that feel longer and less abrupt. That's a possibility, not a promise.

The exercise
For today, just a thought experiment. Notice which thoughts come up when you read the words prostate stimulation. If you like, write them in the app's reframing journal and ask yourself: Is this a fact – or an old image?

When to see a doctor
Pain in the pelvis or perineum, burning when urinating, or blood in the urine or semen should be seen by a doctor before you experiment with touch in this area.
lessons.reflection_question: Which thoughts or old images come up when you think of prostate stimulation – and could you replace them for a moment with curiosity about your own body?

lessons.title: The Perineum: The Bridge From the Outside
lessons.summary: How to reach the root of the erectile tissue and the prostate from the outside via the perineum – a careful, low-shame way in.
lessons.content:
You don't have to start inside to get to know the pleasure of your deep pelvis. Between scrotum and anus lies a bridge of skin a few centimetres long: the perineum.

Why it works
Directly beneath this skin lie the roots of the erectile tissue, pelvic floor muscles and nerve pathways that also lead to the prostate. Touch here combines arousal with grounding: many men experience it as deep and calming at the same time. And because you start from the outside, control stays entirely with you.

The exercise
First, warmth: during your next solo practice or together, put some warm oil or lubricant on your index and middle fingers. Instead of only stroking the shaft, move beneath the testicles onto the perineum.
Second, pressure: about halfway to the anus you'll feel a soft spot. Apply steady, gently pulsing pressure there with two fingertips, inwards and slightly forwards towards the pubic bone.
Third, breath: breathe deeply into your belly and consciously let your pelvic floor sink softly against your fingers. The pelvic floor timer in the app helps you tell contracting and letting go apart. Many men feel a new, dark warmth in the lower body.

Consent and safety
The pressure should be pleasant, never painful. With a partner, the person being touched decides how firm it may be. If pressure on the perineum causes pain, have it checked by a doctor.
lessons.reflection_question: While relaxing today, try placing two fingers calmly on your perineum and breathing deeply into your belly. Can you feel the tissue beneath moving along?

lessons.title: The Way Inside: Slowly, Safely, Without a Goal
lessons.summary: Preparation, hygiene, the exhale trick and the gentle come-hither movement – for a first inner approach to the prostate.
lessons.content:
If you're curious – alone or together – about exploring the prostate directly, three things decide whether it's a good experience: preparation, relaxation and slowness.

Why it works
The sphincter is designed to close when pressed from the outside. Pushing triggers counter-tension and pain – and with it, immediately, the brake from course 1. Working with the breath and giving the body time, on the other hand, opens it from within. The principle of this whole program applies especially clearly here: pressure closes, safety opens.

The exercise
First, preparation: after going to the toilet and taking a shower, the rectum is usually empty. Fingernails short and smooth, hands washed. A disposable glove gives many people a sense of safety. Use plenty of lubricant, because the rectum doesn't lubricate itself.
Second, the exhale: place the oiled fingertip on the outside of the anus without pressing. Breathe in deeply. As you breathe out, let the pelvic floor soften slightly downwards and outwards. Exactly in this moment the finger can slowly glide in a little – or you wait for the next breath.
Third, arriving and moving: about four to five centimetres inside, on the front wall towards the navel, you'll feel a rounded, smooth bulge. That's the prostate. First let the finger rest calmly for a minute and breathe. Then stroke gently over it with the pad of your finger, as if beckoning someone towards you. At the same time the penis can be touched slowly on the outside with a flat hand. The breathing pacer helps you stay calm.
Many need several attempts until it feels good. There is no goal.

Consent and safety
Pain always means: stop. Never insert anything into the anus that doesn't have a flared base and isn't made for it – objects without a stop can slip into the bowel. If you use toys, then silicone ones specifically designed for anal use. After anal contact, wash hands or toys before they touch the vulva or mouth. With a partner: only at their explicit wish, and stoppable at any time.

When to see a doctor
With haemorrhoids, fissures, acute inflammation, after operations in the pelvic area or with persistent pain, ask a doctor first.
lessons.reflection_question: What would you need in terms of time, atmosphere or agreement to allow this experience entirely without pressure, for yourself or with your partner?

lessons.title: Spicy: Prostate Massage From the Inside
lessons.summary: Step by step to the prostate: with a finger or toy, safe, clean and pleasurable.
lessons.content:
The prostate lies about a finger's length inside the anus, towards the navel. For many men its massage is one of the most intense sensations of all; some experience a climax that feels quite different from usual. The key is patience.

Preparation
Relaxation is everything. A warm bath, going to the toilet beforehand, short fingernails, a disposable glove or finger cot, and lots of lube. Silicone lube lasts long but doesn't go with silicone toys.

The way in
Outside first: massage the perineum, circle the anus, press gently without entering. Only when the sphincter feels soft does a finger slide in slowly, on the out-breath. Pause briefly so the body can adjust.

Finding the prostate
The finger curls forwards, towards the navel. After a few centimetres you'll feel a firmer area about the size of a walnut. Stroke there gently, circle or press rhythmically, like a heartbeat. Don't thrust.

With a toy
Prostate toys are curved and always have a wide base so nothing can slip inside. Insert slowly, then play with the pelvic floor: squeeze, release. Some toys move by themselves this way.

Combining
While the prostate is massaged, the other hand can stroke the penis. Many men experience this as especially intense.

Safety
Never go directly from the anus to the vagina or mouth without changing the glove or toy or washing thoroughly. Pain means stop immediately. Get blood or persistent discomfort checked by a doctor.

Extra spicy: how it sounds with dirty talk
“I'm deep inside you.” “Feel your cock twitch when I press here.” “Relax your ass, let me in.” “Come without me touching it.”

The task
Alone or together: take time for the outside part, at least ten minutes, before a finger slides in. The aim isn't climax but finding the prostate and feeling how it responds.
lessons.reflection_question: What helped you relax, and how did the prostate feel?

courses.title: 12. Breaking the Silence
courses.subtitle: How open words dissolve shame and shared calm noticeably lowers the pressure.

lessons.title: Why Hiding Doubles the Pressure
lessons.summary: Why trying not to let anything show is what really fuels the tension.
lessons.content:
When something in bed doesn't go as hoped, the first impulse is often to cover it up, distract, withdraw inwardly. Some go quiet, turn away or make up an excuse.

Why it works
That is deeply human and comes from an old shame: the fear of being seen as not good enough. But hiding costs energy. The mind has to manage two things at once: being aroused and relaxed – and at the same time keeping up a facade so the other person doesn't notice.
This double game presses hard on the brake from course 1. The more you try not to let anything show, the louder your heart pounds. On top of that: without words, the other person often relates the silence to themselves – “Is it me?” That creates pressure on both sides that nobody talks about.
The way out isn't to explain everything, but to be calmly open.

The exercise
Remember a moment when you covered something up. What did you fear would happen if you said it out loud? Write the thought in the reframing journal and check it: How likely is that really? And what would be the worst, the best and the most likely outcome?
The next lesson gives you concrete sentences for exactly these moments.
lessons.reflection_question: How do you typically react after a difficult moment – do you withdraw, or do you talk about it?

lessons.title: Opening the Conversation
lessons.summary: Concrete sentences to raise the topic lightly and in a connecting way – before, during and after.
lessons.content:
Many people don't raise the topic because they fear a long, heavy problem talk. But openness doesn't have to be a drama. It's not about justifying yourself, but about an invitation to relax.

Why it works
A sentence spoken out loud relieves the mind of the double task from the last lesson. It takes away the other person's worry that it's their fault. And it turns a moment of shame into a moment of closeness. Many couples experience exactly this as a turning point.

The exercise
Three sentence templates for three moments. Adapt them to your own way of speaking.
Before, for example while cuddling: “My head is pretty full today. It has nothing to do with you. Let's just kiss and cuddle, with no goal. If more happens, lovely – if not, the closeness is my highlight.”
In the middle, when arousal fades or your heart is racing: “My body needs a little break from the mental movie right now. Let's just lie close and breathe.” Said with a smile, it means: everything is fine.
The next day, over coffee: “Thank you for being so relaxed yesterday. It feels good to know I don't have to put on a show with you.”
Choose one sentence and try it at the next opportunity.

Consent and safety
Openness works both ways. If {P:your partner} confides something like this in you: listen, don't fix, don't play it down. A simple “Thank you for telling me” is enough.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of the three sentences feels most natural for you to try at the next opportunity?

lessons.title: Finding Calm Together
lessons.summary: How two nervous systems can calm each other – and a simple exercise for it.
lessons.content:
Fighting your own restlessness alone in bed leaves you on your own. But humans are built to calm each other. Specialists call this co-regulation.

Why it works
A calm, deep breath next to us often transfers involuntarily to our own rhythm. Warm skin and calm body contact signal safety to the nervous system; the bonding hormone oxytocin also plays a role. Shared calm is therefore one of the most direct ways to release the brake from course 1 – with no performance at all.

The exercise
The shared heart breath. Lie close together. Each of you places a hand on the other's heart. You don't need to talk.
For two minutes, breathe together deeply into the belly and out again very slowly. The app's breathing pacer can set the rhythm.
Notice how your jaw, shoulders and pelvis change over time.
Feel free to suggest the exercise with no sexual intention at all, as a small ritual before falling asleep. That's exactly when it works best.
lessons.reflection_question: Can you imagine suggesting the shared heart breath simply as a cuddling ritual – with no ulterior motive at all?

courses.title: 13. Mismatched Desire: When One Wants It More Often
courses.subtitle: Why desire is rarely evenly distributed – and how to get out of pushing and avoiding.

lessons.title: Not a Defect: Why Desire Is Rarely Evenly Distributed
lessons.summary: Different levels of desire are the normal case in relationships, not the problem.
lessons.content:
One partner would like sex more often, the other less often. In almost every longer relationship this moment comes, and it often feels like a verdict: Something is wrong with me. Or: Something is wrong with us. Both are usually untrue.

Why this happens
Desire isn't a fixed quantity like shoe size. It fluctuates with stress, sleep, health, life phase and the mood in the relationship. Two people who by chance always want the same amount would be the exception.
On top of that, desire can arise in two ways. With spontaneous desire, the wanting comes first, often seemingly out of nowhere. With responsive desire, it only arises once closeness, touch or arousal are already there. Many people, especially in long relationships, mainly experience the responsive form. Those who feel this way rarely think of sex on their own – but can enjoy it a lot when the way in is right.
And finally the dual control model from course 1: desire arises when there is enough accelerator and little on the brake. The partner who wants less often doesn't have too little accelerator, but too much brake: tiredness, pressure, unresolved anger, the feeling of having to perform.

The exercise
Each of you take ten minutes on your own and answer three questions in writing:
When in recent months did I feel desire most – and what was different then?
Do I know spontaneous desire, responsive desire, or both?
What is pressing my brake most right now?
Then share, without discussing. The other only listens and at most asks follow-up questions. The aim isn't to solve a problem, but to understand how desire works for the other.

Consent and safety
Nobody has to justify their desire, whether it's high or low. If your desire has dropped markedly and permanently and that distresses you, it's worth talking to a doctor: hormones, medications such as some antidepressants, the thyroid, depression or pain can be behind it.
lessons.reflection_question: Is your desire more spontaneous or more responsive – and what is pressing your brake right now?

lessons.title: The Vicious Circle of Pushing and Avoiding
lessons.summary: How two loving people take away each other's desire without meaning to.
lessons.content:
Almost every couple with different levels of desire knows this circle: the one who wants more asks, hints, tries. The one who wants less feels pressured and avoids – goes to bed earlier, avoids kisses that might lead somewhere. The other then feels rejected and pushes more. And so on.

Why this happens
Both are acting for good reasons. The one who wants more is often looking not only for sex, but for reassurance: I'm desirable, we're close. That's why every no hits harder than it was meant.
The one who wants less experiences every approach as an expectation. And expectation is a powerful brake pedal. That's why at some point even harmless tenderness disappears, because every touch could seem like an invitation.
The result: one feels unloved, the other under pressure. And both have less closeness than before.

The exercise
First: give the circle a name, for example “our merry-go-round”. When you notice it starting, either of you may say: “We're on the merry-go-round again.” That takes the blame out of the moment.
Second: separate tenderness and sex for two weeks. Kisses, hugs and cuddling are explicitly allowed and explicitly lead nowhere. The one with less desire can then relax again, and the one who wants more still gets closeness.
Third: practise the friendly no. Instead of “No, I'm tired”, for example: “Not for sex tonight, but I'd love to fall asleep in your arms.” A no to sex isn't a no to the person.

Consent and safety
Nobody owes the other sex, and nobody has to beg for closeness. If a no leads to accusations, silence or pressure, that's a topic for a calm conversation or couples counselling.
lessons.reflection_question: How do you notice that you're on the merry-go-round – and what could you do differently next time?

lessons.title: The Pleasure Menu: More Than Yes or No
lessons.summary: Having more options between sex and nothing means saying yes more often.
lessons.content:
Many couples know only two options: sex or nothing. Anyone not in the mood for the full programme then simply says no. A pleasure menu opens up the space in between.

Why it works
The partner with less desire often isn't rejecting closeness, but the prospect of something big, long and strenuous. With small, clearly limited invitations, the brake is much quieter. And because responsive desire only arises along the way, a small invitation sometimes turns into more – without it having to.

The exercise
Together, write a menu with three sections.
Starters, five to ten minutes: for example long kisses, showering together, lying naked and cuddled up, a neck massage.
Main courses: touch without a goal like the shared evening in this app, a hand job for one of you, oral sex, sex.
Desserts for low-energy days: one touches themselves while the other holds them, or simply falling asleep together.
Each of you marks what you currently like, what maybe, what not. Hang the menu somewhere only you two see it, or save it on your phone.
From now on the invitation is no longer “Do you feel like it?”, but “Would you like something from the menu?”. And the partner with less desire may choose too: “A starter works tonight.”

Consent and safety
A starter is a starter. Choosing it doesn't promise a main course. That's exactly what makes the menu safe. If you'd like ideas: the yes/no/maybe list in the couple channel helps fill it.
lessons.reflection_question: What's on your personal starter menu – small things you could almost always say yes to?

lessons.title: Conditions for Desire: What Releases Your Brake
lessons.summary: Desire itself can't be planned – but the circumstances under which it can arise can.
lessons.content:
Desire can't be ordered. But you can create the conditions under which it arises more easily. For the partner with less desire, this is often the most important lever.

Why it works
When the brake is the problem, more accelerator doesn't help much. An even more seductive offer changes nothing when the head is full of appointments or an argument from yesterday is still echoing. Knowing your brakes and making them smaller together gives desire room.
Time set aside for closeness also has a bad reputation it doesn't deserve. A fixed evening removes the uncertainty about whether and when it will happen, and gives time to arrive. Many couples experience scheduled evenings as more relaxed.

The exercise
Each of you writes two lists. My brakes: what takes my desire away, for example an untidy bedroom, tiredness, the feeling that sex is expected, unresolved anger. My accelerator: what awakens desire, for example time without phones, a conversation, having laughed together, being freshly showered, compliments that don't want anything.
Read your lists to each other. Then choose one brake per person that you can make smaller together, and one accelerator you'll build in this week.
If you like, agree on one evening a week as your time: with no obligation to have sex, but with time for closeness. The shared evening in the app can be a start.

Consent and safety
The lists are gifts, not demands. If you notice you can't get further on your own, couples or sex counselling isn't a sign of failure, but often the quickest way back to each other.
lessons.reflection_question: Which one brake could you make smaller together this week?

courses.title: 14. Life Phases: Desire in Transition
courses.subtitle: After birth, in menopause, over the years and in illness – what changes and what helps.

lessons.title: After Birth: A New Body, a New Couple
lessons.summary: Why desire often takes a break after giving birth – and how closeness can stay anyway.
lessons.content:
After giving birth, much is different: the body, sleep, everyday life, your role as a couple. That sex moves into the background for a while is not a warning sign, but entirely ordinary.

Why this happens
The body is healing. Birth injuries, a caesarean or an overstretched pelvic floor need time. While breastfeeding, oestrogen levels are low. As a result the mucous membranes are often drier and more sensitive, and desire can be quieter. On top of that come lack of sleep and the feeling of having been touched all day already.
The partner also experiences the new time differently: some long for closeness as reassurance, others are exhausted or unsure themselves.

The exercise
First: talk about closeness, not just about sex. What are you both missing right now? Often it's time for two, a conversation that isn't about the baby, a hug without ulterior motives.
Second: when you want to sleep together again, start slowly. Plenty of water-based lubricant, positions in which the woman sets depth and pace, and permission to stop at any time.
Third: release the pelvic floor first, then strengthen it. The pelvic floor timer in the app starts with letting go, which is also the right way in after giving birth.

Consent and safety
